claims.text: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment inherently contain grain boundaries and surface porosity that permit attack by molten aluminum.
A sol-gel-deposited aluminum precursor can be converted by thermal oxidation into a continuous, dense alumina surface layer.
The proposed treatment forms a sub-micron alumina layer.
The proposed alumina layer is adherent and dense.
The alumina layer reduces surface porosity and seals grain-boundary defects in the boride substrate.
Dense alumina physically and chemically blocks interaction between molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate.
Alumina has sufficient chemical stability and sufficiently low diffusivity at approximately 660 °C to impede aluminum penetration and reaction.
Impeding aluminum penetration and reaction suppresses molten-aluminum corrosion of the boride component.
Alumina-coated boride components will exhibit lower corrosion-associated weight change than untreated boride components after equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
Alumina-coated boride components will exhibit less aluminum infiltration than untreated components.
Alumina-coated boride components will exhibit less microstructural degradation than untreated components.
Untreated boride-based components undergo measurable weight change and microstructural damage during standard molten-aluminum exposure cycles.
The protective improvement should persist while the alumina coating remains intact and defect-free.
Mechanical or thermal coating damage can compromise the protective effect.
Temperatures substantially above 660 °C or exposure longer than normal plating cycles may compromise coating efficacy.
Molten-aluminum exposure at approximately 660 °C is representative of hot-dip aluminum-plating operation.
The magnitude of corrosion reduction and the long-term stability of the alumina layer under cyclic thermal and mechanical stress have not been quantitatively established.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing coated and untreated boride samples under identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
Weight change, SEM/EDS infiltration measurements, profilometric corrosion depth, microstructural damage, and coating adhesion can be used as experimental response variables.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in weight change, infiltration depth, or microstructural damage relative to untreated controls would reject the hypothesis.
